title: Shipping something to someone always wins — Kenneth Auchenberg (ex. Stripe, VSCode)
talk_summary: A product-management talk arguing that the number of fast iteration loops with real users matters more than big-bang launches, illustrated by the skateboard-to-car metaphor and Stripe/VSCode anecdotes.

takeaways.technique: Sub-day feedback loop as a hard process constraint
takeaways.what_they_do: Before locking design decisions, they require a loop where real users see something, feedback comes back, and an improvement ships — all in under a day.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you cannot run your loop in a day, your process is broken

takeaways.technique: Write the launch post / PR-FAQ before building
takeaways.what_they_do: They draft the press release, FAQ, or launch blog post and API outline and send it to early users for feedback before any prototype exists.
takeaways.evidence_quote: writing the PI FAQ or the press release or the blog post forces you to write something specific

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of relying on metrics dashboards, they shadow users, put them in Slack/Discord, and watch API responses to see exactly where people get stuck.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it's very easy to slap slap on some metrics and build a dashboard, but doesn't help you get get any quality feedback

takeaways.technique: Professional-services mode for a tiny user set
takeaways.what_they_do: Early on they deliberately serve a very small set of users extremely well, acting like a bespoke services firm, rather than optimizing for breadth.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it should feel like you're running a professional services firm for your customers in the early days

takeaways.what_they_do: When teams stall in debate, they build a quick prototype (now with AI/v0) and let real feedback settle the argument instead of more discussion.
takeaways.evidence_quote: shipping something to someone always wins and solves a debate when you get real feedback from real people
